posts.cooked:
We're arguing about how to resolve the timing of the steps on the card.  In some cases, when an effect happens is absolutely critical.

Hypersonic assault (for instance) caused a debate, because there are targets that deal damage in retaliation, or in response to cards being destroyed (such as the chairman dealing damage when being hit, or the Matriarch hitting when birds are destroyed).

The debate centered around WHEN the secondary effect (targets can't deal damage) happened- did it happen as soon as a target was dealt damage?  did it happen after ALL targets were dealt damage?

If you resolved the entire card one target at a time (which was the eventual ruling), then you could pull off a lot of fun tricks like hitting the Matriarch first (so that she couldn't deal damage), and then taking out her entire army of birds with the rest of Hypersonic Assault.

 

In response to your question:  

you can apply the additional damage to multiple targets.  You do this one target at a time- deal a target 1 energy, then if it took damage, you decide if you are going to deal it 1 more energy damage.  Once this is accomplished for one target, move on to the next target.

Case A (Foote) is this: KNYFE hits a target, then immediately acts on the second sentence, and chooses whether or not to hit them again, and THEN moves on to the second target, repeating this process for each target. Let's just call this "Option A," for solidarity and consistancy and whatever.

 

Case B (Skippy) is this: KNYFE hits every target, and THEN goes through and decides which ones she wants to hit them a second time. Let's call this "Option B."

 

Personally, I think A has the most evidence, as the official ruling for Hypersonic Assault (which had basically the exact same formatting of "hit everybody. something happens to whoever took damage this way." ) was that the second sentence (targets that take damage this way cannot deal damage) triggered IMMEDIATELY upon the dealing of the damage, and someone with retaliations like The Chairman or Miss Information would instantly be blocked from counterattacking, rather than being able to hit back if you weren't done hitting every target in play. Therefore, this card should work the same way; you hit something, and then -- because it took damage -- you are immediately granted the option of hitting it again.

posts.name: Braithwhite
posts.cooked:
the only time I can see this being really important (as we are dealing strictly with damage as a seconidary effect) is when enemies that grant damage resistance are in play.  To keep this simple, we should assume that in this example, the enemy grants damage resistance to everything except itself (or else you have to get clever with buffs/flawless execution/nattering about with how much HP it has...)

 

Case A: Hit enemy granting damage resistance (to other things, not itself) 1 time.  Hit enemy granting damage resistance again.  (killing enemy granting damage resistance).

Move to the next target (which no longer benefits from damage resistance granted by slain enemy).

 

Case B: Hit enemy granting damage resistance (to other things, not itself) (it lives).  Move to the next target, which has damage resistance (dealing no damage), then subsequent targets (dealing no damage, as they are protected by the first one), then hero/environment targets.

THEN, you may deal 1 point to the enemy providing damage resistance (to other things, not itself), killing it.  Unfortunately, all other (non-hero) targets were protected during the first wave of damage, so you can't choose to deal them anything.

 

In this set of examples, the first option (dealing damage one step at a time, one target at a time) is more flexible, as it allows you to pick off targets that might otherwise protect or prevent you from dealing damage.

a) If you do, then you are falling under the fiddlyiness of competitive card gaming - where the exact wording on a card, if slightly different than another, may make the difference between winning and not winning because of the order in which an effect occurs. This is because those games are competitive and only one person wins. 'the wording on these two cards is not 100% identical' is a common line of reasoning from such types of players. This is why games like Magic and L5R strive so hard to have a formal template on how to word cards, something like price ; effect so all cards are worded with a semicolon between price and effect (not that that is the format, but its an example)

 

b) if you don't play those, well you're still falling under that fiddlyiness. Remember. SotM is a co-operative card game. It also does not have a formal template for wording on cards, but its meant to be taken with a healthy does of 'what feels right' - These two cards are very similar in manner - do one thing successfully, and if you did that thing do another thing - the wordings may be different, but the feel is the same, and because we've had rulling on high about one such card, it applies to all similar cards, even if the wording isnt exactly 100% similar.

Let me try a different track

Thats  because you're still following the thought process that the wording has to be 100% the same in order to have the same effect.  I am a very big LCG/CCG player - years of magic, currently L5R, and Android Netrunner, and these fiddly not exactly the same wording situations will mean a card interacts differently - because we always have to play with Read as Written  (RaW) - you can't look at a card and see what the designer intended, because what I think and what my opponent across the table thinks may be two different things, and in a game where there can only be one winner, this is a big problem. However reading it straight up logically in a manner that (most) people agree is the same reading (or better yet with evidence from other, same worded cards) doesn't allow for one player to think they won and the other to think so as well. This is Read as Written. with RaW you are exactly right - if they are not 100% the same wording, then they will act differently.

 


Luckily here, we have Christopher on hand, and also not being a Competitive game, we can very certainly Read as Intended (RaI) because we can make inferences based on what we know of Christopher and he can even give us inputs. Then because it is not competitive, no one is hurt if one group plays it one way and another group plays it slightly different. Sure if those two groups get together there may be a disagreement, but even then - the players are still going to win or loose together, not one group is going to win and the other is going to loose because of a disagreement of wording.  The intent behind this card was for it to act similarly to Hypersonic Assault. Because we already have a rulling on that card, we can apply that same rulling here, because RaI shows them to be similar action cards, and under RaI wording is not as important as the overall effects of the card itself.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
I am not following the wording alone, but the steps that wording cause to take place.

 

Hypersonic Assault does not involve a choice.

Hypersonic assault does not involve a seperate effect.

The Second line of Hypersonic Assault is a modification, it modifies the effect of the first line.

A second instance of damage is not a modification of an instance of damage.

A second instance of damage is a seperate effect.

It makes a much better comparison to Pride and Prejudice than Hypersonic assault.

Just Like Shock Rounds is not a modification of the damage dealt by the gun it is loaded in.  It is a seperate effect, triggered by the first effect.

 

Another comparison I would make is Imbued Fire vs. Twist the Ether.

The cause is damage being dealt by a qualifying dealer.

The effect of Imbued Fire is a modification of that damage.

The effect of Twist the Ether is a choice of effects.

 

There is not a perfect comparison for this game, but there are far better comparisons than Hypersonic Assault, and certainly they are not similar enough to use the same ruling.

I have no disagreement with how the card officially resolves.  It makes sense.

But it does not fall under a ruling from a card that different than it mechanically.

In fact, i think the reason you are having trouble with applying the Hypersonic Ruling to this card is because you possibly are seeing the ruling as 'If you have a card that gives you two effects, the second one being a modifier of the first ... (ect into the ruling)'

 

Where as the rulling is better thought of 'If you have a card that simultaneously applies multiple effects to multiple targets, players may apply both effects at once to each target before moving on to the next' -  Both of these cards have more than one (multiple) effects that apply to multiple targets, so the ruling is that players get to apply them both at the same time to each target before moving on - KNYFE gets a May conditional in that, but it still is both effects at once.

Even if it isn't competitive, I feel that it's appropriate that it should have the same strictness of templating that competitive games use, so that you can be sure that you really earn your victories by playing the game exactly right.  Every time I make a mistake, I feel dumb about it; I would be happier if the game were as airtight and idiot-proof as possible, so that I could always be sure that the credit for victory or fault for defeat lies solely upon myself and the other players (and Lady Luck), our strategic and tactical decisions, not just our ability to make rules calls in our own favor.

EDIT - I do however agree with the logic of your second post, that we can get answers straight from Christopher or just use a "gut impression" of what he was probably going for, based on past rulings.  In a lot of cases, that's good enough.  Given that my superhero ID is "The Perfectionist", I always wish it could be better, but what we have is certainly better than what Magic has, where there's a guy at WOTCO HQ whose entire job is to constantly find fault with the rulings and publish a quarterly report of updated wordings.
